questions.q: Why do AI SDKs ask you to construct a client object once (with your API key) instead of passing the API key to every individual function call?
options: It's required by Python syntax rules
It avoids repeating credentials and config on every call — the client stores them once via __init__ and self
It makes the API key get sent in plain text
It prevents the SDK from making more than one request
questions.explain: This is the same __init__/self pattern from Lesson 13: the client object stores credentials and config as instance attributes once, and every method call afterward reuses that stored state.

questions.q: What advantage does a dataclass-based response object have over a raw dictionary returned from an API call?
options: Dictionaries are always faster
A dataclass can hold unlimited fields while a dictionary cannot
Typed fields (like response.text) let editors autocomplete and catch typos, rather than a misspelled dict key silently returning None
There's no real advantage; it's purely stylistic
questions.explain: A dataclass response gives named, typed attributes. Misspelling response.text as response.txt is caught immediately, whereas response['txt'] on a raw dict just returns a KeyError or silently misses depending on how it's accessed.

questions.q: Given `class RateLimitError(AIError): pass`, what does `except AIError:` catch?
options: Only errors of the exact type AIError, never RateLimitError
Nothing, since AIError is never actually raised directly
RateLimitError, and any other exception that inherits from AIError, thanks to inheritance
Only built-in Python exceptions, never custom ones
questions.explain: This is Lesson 14's inheritance applied to exceptions: catching a parent exception class also catches every exception type that inherits from it.

questions.q: Which Lesson 13-15 concept does a 'client object' (constructed once, reused for every API call) correspond to?
options: Dataclass equality (__eq__)
frozen=True immutability
__init__ storing state on self, so it persists across method calls
Multiple inheritance from several parent classes
questions.explain: A client object is a direct application of Lesson 13: __init__ sets instance attributes (like api_key) via self, and those attributes remain available to every method called on that instance afterward.

questions.q: Why would an SDK bother building a hierarchy of error classes (AIError -> RateLimitError, AuthenticationError, etc.) instead of just raising one generic Exception for everything?
options: It lets calling code choose to catch errors broadly (AIError) or specifically (just RateLimitError, to retry) depending on what it needs to do
Python requires at least three custom exception classes per package
It makes the SDK's code run faster
Generic exceptions are not allowed in Python
questions.explain: An error hierarchy gives calling code flexibility: catch the narrow, specific error type to handle it precisely (e.g., retry on RateLimitError), or catch the broad base type to handle any AI-related failure in one place.
